processing: A blend of finished teas, not a processing style: a smooth Chinese black such as Keemun is combined with a proportion of pine-smoked Lapsang Souchong and often a roasted oolong, in varying ratios, so the smoke sits in the background rather than dominating.
harvest_season: Not a harvest: blended year-round from stock teas, whose own spring harvests set the base quality.
appearance_dry: Mixed dark twisted leaf, some glossy black, some brown, with a faint pine-smoke and dried-fruit smell.
appearance_wet: Dark copper and brown leaf with a soft smoky scent.
taste_profile: Gently smoky and malty with a sweet, dried-fruit base and a roasted, woody edge; mellower than straight Lapsang, with the Keemun's cocoa and the oolong's roundness showing through.

brewing.notes: Just-boiled water, 3–4 minutes; it takes milk or lemon but is best plain. A second steep is thinner but keeps the smoke. If the blend is heavy on Lapsang, shorten the steep rather than diluting.

vintage_note: No vintage and no harvest year: a year-round blend with a two- to three-year best-before, and the smoke fades first, so an open tin is best within a year. The ratio of smoked to unsmoked tea is the whole character and varies from a whisper to a dominant note, so the label and a sniff of the tin are the guide; serious blenders name the components (Keemun, Lapsang Souchong, oolong), supermarket versions may use smoke flavouring instead of smoked leaf. The name recalls the caravan route.
description:
Russian Caravan is a blend with a romantic name: Chinese black tea, a measure of pine-smoked Lapsang Souchong and often some oolong, meant to evoke the tea that reached Russia overland by camel caravan through Mongolia and Siberia from the eighteenth century. The story that the smoke came from the caravans' campfires is a legend; the smoke comes from Lapsang, and who first made the blend is unclear.

There is no processing to describe, only a recipe. The base is usually a smooth, slightly cocoa-like Keemun, the smoke is Lapsang Souchong, and a roasted oolong or a Yunnan black is often added for roundness; the blender's choice of ratio makes the difference between a subtle, savoury tea and a bonfire.

Brewed three to four minutes it is gently smoky, malty and sweet with a dried-fruit base and a woody finish, more approachable than straight Lapsang and good with savoury food, smoked fish, cheese or a full breakfast. It takes a little milk, but most people who like it drink it plain. The mistake is treating it like a breakfast tea and stewing it; the smoke turns acrid.

It is sold year-round without a vintage, loose and in bags, and the only things worth checking are the named components and whether the smoke is real smoked leaf or a flavouring. Russian tea culture itself, incidentally, is mostly about strong black tea from the samovar, not smoke.

If you like it, go to the sources: a plain Keemun, a lightly smoked Tongmu Lapsang, and then blend your own to taste.
history:
The name looks back to the camel caravans that, from the eighteenth century, carried tea overland from the Chinese border across Mongolia and Siberia to European Russia. The journey took at least half a year. Russian connoisseurs paid extra for caravan tea, believing that the cold, dry route improved it and that the moisture it took up at night on the snowy steppe gave it delicacy.

The usual story says the smoky taste came from the caravans' campfires. The smoke in the modern blend comes from lapsang souchong, and some versions leave it out altogether.

Today's recipe is oolong, keemun and lapsang souchong, with Yunnan black or Assam in some blends. Who first blended it is unclear; one account has Russians reworking imported Chinese black tea to their own taste.
